Male urethral diverticulum without having urethral stricture: A rare case 
Jalil Hosseini, Ali Goudarzi Karim, Amir Reza Abedi * 
Men’s Health and Reproductive Health Research Center, Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Urethral diverticulum 
Urethra 
Surgery 
A B S T R A C T   
A rare case of male urethral diverticulum presents in this article. A 34-year-old man was referred to our clinic 
because of post-void dribbling. The retrograde cystogram and cystoscopy confirmed a 3 cm urethral diverticulum 
in the penile urethra without having urethra stricture. Open surgical repair was scheduled to excise urethral 
diverticulum and restore urethral continuity. Corpus spongiosum and dartus fascia was used to reinforce the 
repair.   
1. Introduction 
A urethral diverticulum (UD) is a saccular dilation that is connected 
with the true urethral lumen with a narrow or a wide neck. It is a rare 
problem in men that can be congenital or acquired. There are a few case 
reports or case series about male urethral diverticula, so the prevalence 
of urethral diverticula is unknown in men.1 Most acquired UDs result 
from urethral stricture, trauma, or infection.2 There are reports about 
UDs that are secondary to prostate surgery, surgical implants, hypo­
spadias repair, urethroplasty, and indwelling urethral catheter. UDs play 
as a nidus for urine stasis that cause recurrent urinary infection, stone 
formation, and urinary leakage.1 We present a rare case with a penile 
urethral diverticulum without having urethral stricture or surgery. 
2. Case presentation 
A 34-year-old man was referred to the urology clinic located in 
Shohada-e Tajrish hospital. The patient complained about post void 
urinary leakage, terminal dribbling, and difficult ejaculation. The pa­
tient has not had any history of anterior urethral valves/previous uro­
logic history in the past. He had a car accident three years ago for which 
explorative laparotomy was done at that time. Physical examination 
demonstrated a penoscrotal mass that bulged during voiding (Fig. 1). 
Retrograde urethrogram was scheduled (Fig. 2), then cystoscopy was 
performed that showed a 3cm urethral diverticula located 9 cm distal to 
meatus in the penile urethra. Surgical repair was scheduled. Under 
general anesthesia, longitudinal incision was made in the ventral side of 
penis. The urethra was mobilized off the underlying corpora in a normal- 
appearing region. This dissection was carried proximally, and ventrally

we encountered the diverticulum. Longitudinal incision was made on 
the diverticula that revealed large thin urethra. Trimming of the thin 
urethra was done in order to create a normal caliber urethra (Fig. 3). The 
tissue, which was trimmed, was sent to the pathology department. Then 
We re-approximated the remaining urethral tissue off-tension in the 
typical fashion with Vicryl suture 3/0 (Ethicon), and was supported by 
corpus spongiosum and three other layers derived from dartus fascia. We

reconstructed the urethra as wide as a two-way foley catheter 18 F. 
Finally, Open cystostomy was placed. The patient has been followed, his 
penoscrotal bulge was disappeared, but he reports some degree of uri­
nary incontinence. 
3. Discussion 
Male urethral diverticulum is a rare finding, and it results from 
urethral stricture, infection, or trauma.2 Three causative mechanisms 
have been suggested for acquired male urethral diverticulum: 1- the 
most common underlying cause is related to urethral obstruction; for 
example, this mechanism explains how urethral diverticulum develops 
after hypospadias repair or reconstructive procedures for urethral 
stricture3 2- the second mechanism is related to continuous pressure 
distributed on the penoscrotal angle which causes urethral ischemia and 
fibrosis; for instance, this mechanism is seen in patients who develop 
urethral diverticulum after indwelling urethral catheterization4 3- the 
third mechanism is related to anorectal malformation repair.5 Our pa­
tient had a car accident while he was riding a motorcycle. The patient

was being dragged on the ground. His penis was pressed against the 
ground; as a result, corpus spongiosum most likely has been necrosed, 
and then atrophied, so the urethra mucosa herniated through the defect 
and urethra diverticula developed. 
The treatment of male urethral diverticulum is based on patient 
symptoms, the size and thickness of the urethral diverticulum wall.1 The 
patients who have a small and asymptomatic urethral diverticulum do 
not need surgical repair. These cases can be managed with post-void 
manual milking of urethral diverticulum in order to avoid urinary sta­
sis. Most of these patients need long-term prophylactic antibiotic to keep 
urine sterile and close follow-up.4 Endoscopic treatment of urethral 
diverticulum has not been recommended.1,2 Open surgical repair has 
been suggested as the best approach in order to manage urethral 
diverticulum; the goal of surgical repair is to excise urethral diverticula 
(8). Local urethral or penile flaps can be used to reinforce the repair, but 
extragenital grafts such as buccal grafts can be used for the larger defect 
of urethral lumen.1,3 We provide corpus spongiosum and dartus flaps to 
reinforce the repair so as to reduce the risk of urethrocutaneous fistula.
